# Session 7 · Protect & write: ethics, integrity, Methods and Results

## Week 7 · Saturday, 19:30-22:30 (online)

- 19:30  Recap: Session 6
- 19:40  7.1  Protocol, ethics, consent, registration, feasibility
- 20:10  7.2  Research integrity: authorship, conflicts of interest, data sharing, AI
- 20:30  Proposal builder 7: ethics and publication plan
- 21:00  7.3  Writing the paper (I): IMRaD, Methods and Results
- 21:35  Manuscript workshop 1: the Results section of your own question

::: {.notes}
Session 7 (19:30-22:30, break 20:45-21:00). Before the break: ethics, integrity and Proposal Part 4. After the break: IMRaD, Methods and Results.

Two days before the session, email the exercise sheet, the five results packs, the manuscript template and the list of reviewer pairs (drawn at random).

If time is short, drop extra slides, never the workshop.
:::

## Recap quiz: Session 6 in five questions

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 8 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A crude OR (odds ratio) is 2.1. The adjusted OR is 1.4. What happened?
- HR (hazard ratio) 0.85, 95% CI (confidence interval) 0.60 to 1.20: a clear benefit?
- Lactate is missing for 15% of patients. Name one way to handle it
- Kaplan-Meier curve: what does a 'censored' patient mean?
- The FLUID-ICU question you chose (Q1 to Q5): what is its main result? Answer in the chat
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Questions 1 to 4 in the poll. Question 5 in the chat
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap (19:30-19:40). Start with two or three Session 6 exit answers.

Questions 1-4: 30 seconds each in the poll. Show the results, then the next slide, and ask one volunteer why.

Question 5 in the chat: the main result of the question each person chose. Anyone without a question chooses one now.
:::

## Recap quiz: answers

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Confounding]{.neu-card-title}

- Part of the crude link
- came from severity
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[No]{.neu-card-title}

- The CI includes 1
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Two options]{.neu-card-title}

- Complete-case analysis
- or multiple imputation with a sensitivity analysis
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Censored]{.neu-card-title}

- Left the study alive
- The outcome after that is unknown
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Confounding, CIs, missing data and censoring all come back in your Results.
:::

::: {.notes}
The four answers on one slide. Question 1 leads to today: the Results report both crude and adjusted estimates.

Timing: within the 8 minutes of the recap.
:::

## Today: finish the proposal, start the paper

::: {.neu-intro}
FLUID-ICU = the course dataset: a simulated cohort of 620 adults with sepsis in 4 ICUs (Sessions 5-6).

Top row, Product 1: the proposal on your own question. Parts 1 to 3 are done. Today: Part 4. Session 8: submit it, and about 5 people present.

Bottom row, Product 2: the Results section of your FLUID-ICU question (Q1 to Q5). We give the results, you write. Today: Methods and Results. Session 8: the other sections. After the course: peer review and revision. Only the Results must be submitted.

Bottom strip: the two example papers, sent as PDFs.

Ask: which question (Q1-Q5) have you chosen?

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Your four proposal parts are the skeleton of a protocol.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture is a house. The roof is the protocol, the four pillars are the four proposal parts, and the base says it is approved before the first patient and then followed.

Walk the pillars: who and what (title page), why (Part 1), how (Parts 2-3), protect and share (Part 4, today).

SPIRIT 2025 (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) is the checklist for trial protocols. Paper 1 registered its protocol and statistical analysis plan (SAP) before the first patient (NCT04947904).

Poll: which part of your proposal is weakest? Expected: sample size or analysis plan.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Helsinki says why we protect participants. GCP says how we run a trial well.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two panels, six principles each, one icon per principle.

Left, the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2024): the participant comes before new knowledge. Ethics approval, free consent, privacy, registration, publish all results.

Right, Good Clinical Practice (GCP), the International Council for Harmonisation guideline ICH E6(R3), 2025: the quality standard for trials. Paper 1, an academic trial, followed it.

Poll: which of the 12 points would be hardest in our unit?
:::

## The ethics-committee journey: approval before data

::: {.neu-intro}
Plan 1 to 3 months. Questions and revisions from the committee are normal.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** No approval letter, no data collection: not even 'just a few patients'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Six steps, left to right, each with an icon: prepare, review, submit, decide, approve, start. The orange loop shows that questions from the committee send you back to revise and resubmit.

Most institutions want a scientific review first. The committee decides the review type, not you.

The red box: no data before the approval letter. Misconception: 'collect now, ask later'. Committees cannot approve retrospectively.

The grey box: approval is not the end. Amendments, adverse events and reports go to the committee during the study.

Paper 1 gives its approval number in the Methods.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Trials must register, reviews are expected to, observational studies should.
:::

::: {.notes}
Top row: the order of events. Registration comes after ethics approval and before the first participant.

Three columns: clinical trials (mandatory, ClinicalTrials.gov or another World Health Organization (WHO) primary registry), systematic reviews (expected, on PROSPERO, the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews), observational studies (recommended).

Registration puts the study and its primary outcome on public record before anyone is enrolled.

Bottom bar: Paper 1 registered on 1 July 2021 and enrolled its first patient in September 2021.

Ask: does your study need registration?
:::

## Informed consent: four essentials

::: {.neu-intro}
Consent is a conversation, not a signature.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Informed]{.neu-card-title}

- Purpose and what will happen
- Risks, benefits, alternatives
- How data are protected
- Who to contact
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Understood]{.neu-card-title}

- Plain, local language
- Time to ask questions
- Teach-back: 'tell me in your words'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Voluntary]{.neu-card-title}

- No pressure
- Free to refuse or withdraw
- Care is not affected
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Documented]{.neu-card-title}

- Signed and dated form
- A copy for the participant
- Re-consent if the study changes
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** If the patient cannot explain the study back to you, consent is not informed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four cards: valid consent needs information, understanding, voluntariness and a record.

In Paper 1, two control patients withdrew and were not analysed: the right respected.

Ask: who takes consent in your study, and when? Expected: a trained team member, not the treating doctor under time pressure.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Trials: always. Extra data collection: usually. Routine data: may be waived.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three columns, from most to least contact with the patient.

Clinical trials: always. The study decides the treatment, so the patient, the legal representative, or (in the ICU, if approved) deferred consent is needed. Paper 1 did this.

Prospective observational studies that add samples or data beyond routine care (an extra blood test, a questionnaire, a follow-up call): usually yes.

Retrospective studies, or studies of routinely collected data only: the committee may waive consent. If an earlier study's consent form allowed reuse of the data for future analyses, that consent covers it. Paper 2 (a registry) had a waiver.

Bottom bar: the ethics committee decides, not the researcher. The plan goes in the protocol.

Ask: FLUID-ICU used routine chart data only. Which column? Expected: the third, the committee may waive consent.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Patient, then legal representative, then deferred consent (only if approved).
:::

::: {.notes}
The flowchart asks three questions from left to right. Green: someone consents. Orange: deferred consent. Red: do not enrol.

Most ICU patients cannot decide when they become eligible. Patient, then legal representative, then deferred consent only if the committee approved it in advance.

Bottom boxes: Paper 1 (randomised trial) used this route. Paper 2 (registry) had a waiver of the patients' consent.

Local law decides who may be the representative.

Ask: the family refuses after enrolment. What happens? Expected: the patient leaves the study.
:::

## Worked example: who consents for these three ICU patients?

::: {.neu-intro}
Walk each patient through the flowchart on the previous slide.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Mr A, 54]{.neu-card-title}

- Pneumonia, awake, oriented
- Eligible for a fluid trial
- **[Patient consents]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Mrs B, 71]{.neu-card-title}

- Septic shock, sedated
- Daughter at the bedside
- **[Representative consents. Ask Mrs B when awake]{style="color:#2E8B57"}**
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Mr C, 38]{.neu-card-title}

- Septic shock at 03:00, no family yet
- Treatment cannot wait, committee approved
- **[Deferred consent: ask as soon as possible]{style="color:#D9822B"}**
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Awake: the patient. Sedated: the representative. No one, urgent: deferred consent.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three patients, one card each, with the answer in colour at the bottom.

For each patient, call on someone to walk them through the flowchart.

Mr A: consents himself. Mrs B: the representative consents, ask her when she can decide. Mr C: deferred consent, only if approved.

Misconception: the treating doctor can consent for the patient. No.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Analyse coded data. Keep the identifying file locked and apart.
:::

::: {.notes}
Left table: three patients as the ward knows them. Name, hospital number and birth date (red) identify them, so they stay on the ward.

Right table: the same patients after coding: a study code, age instead of birth date, month instead of the exact date. The fluid balance is unchanged.

The identifying file (key icon) holds the link between each study code and the patient. It is locked, kept apart, with one or two named people.

Why names stay on the ward: the analysis does not need them, and a lost laptop or email then reveals nobody.

Bottom left, pseudonymised data: coded, but the link still exists. Used during the study for data checks and follow-up.

Bottom right, anonymised data: the link is destroyed and nobody can trace a patient. Used to share data outside the team. With very small groups (n \< 5), even anonymised data can point to one patient.

No patient data on personal phones, messaging apps or public AI tools.

Ask: where would your identifying file live?
:::

## Worked example: the ethics paragraph for a cohort like FLUID-ICU

::: {.neu-intro}
FLUID-ICU is simulated. If it were real, this is what the paper would say.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Approval]{.neu-card-title}

- Ethics committee of each ICU
- Approval number and date
- Before data collection
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Patient's consent]{.neu-card-title}

- Routine data, minimal risk
- The committee may waive it, as it did for Paper 2 (registry data)
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Confidentiality]{.neu-card-title}

- Study codes only
- Identifying file kept in each ICU
- Data de-identified before analysis
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Registration and sharing]{.neu-card-title}

- Registration recommended, for example on ClinicalTrials.gov
- Data-sharing statement
- Data dictionary shared
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Your manuscript's ethics paragraph answers four questions in four sentences.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four cards, one sentence each: approval, the patient's consent, confidentiality, registration and sharing.

Consent: FLUID-ICU used routine chart data only, so the committee could waive the patient's consent, as it did for Paper 2.

Ask: where does this paragraph go in a real paper? Expected: the Methods.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Check time, budget, people, recruitment and data before you commit.
:::

::: {.notes}
Five columns, one question each.

Timeline: a Gantt chart has one bar per task across the months, so overlaps and delays are easy to see. Ethics alone takes 1-3 months. Recruitment takes longer than planned.

Budget: study staff, materials and tests, the publication fee. People: who collects data at night, who analyses, and is there time freed from clinical work?

Recruitment: the funnel. Paper 1 screened 1,201 patients to randomise 50 (4%) in 17 months.

Data: is it recorded routinely? Prevent missing data first, then plan for the gaps you cannot avoid. Paper 2 had no diuretic data.

Rule of thumb: count last year's eligible patients and expect to enrol a fraction.

Poll: which column is the biggest risk for your study?
:::

Research integrity
:::

Honest data, honest credit, honest use of AI
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 7.2 (20:10-20:30). Six slides, then a 5-minute scenario poll.

Tone: most integrity problems start as small shortcuts under pressure.

Every Results draft needs the AI-use statement.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Never invent, change or copy. Report missing data as missing.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three panels, each with a small picture.

Fabrication: real values (45) and invented ones (red question marks), written in with a pencil.

Falsification: a scatter plot with two inconvenient points struck out.

Plagiarism: lines copied from one page to another without credit.

Bottom bar: these three (FFP) are research misconduct. An honest error is not: correct it openly.

The data-quality plan from Session 5 protects against accidental falsification.

Poll: which is most common in student theses? Expected: plagiarism.
:::

## Also off-limits: tricks that distort the record

::: {.neu-intro}
One study should tell one complete, honest story.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Duplicate publication]{.neu-card-title}

- Same results published twice
- The second paper does not say so
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Salami slicing]{.neu-card-title}

- One study cut into thin papers
- Done to multiply publications
- The reader never sees the whole
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Selective reporting]{.neu-card-title}

- Only the 'significant' outcomes reported
- Primary outcome switched after seeing the data
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Register first, pre-specify the primary outcome, report all of it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three cards. Duplicate publication counts the same patients twice. Salami slicing hides the whole study. Selective reporting is why trials register one primary outcome.

Paper 1 reported its negative primary outcome plainly.

Ask: why does it matter that a negative trial is published? Expected: publication bias.
:::

## Who is an author? The four ICMJE criteria

::: {.neu-intro}
International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE): an author meets all four.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** All four criteria, for every author. Decide the list at the start.
:::

::: {.notes}
The picture is a sum: criterion 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = author. Each criterion has an icon: an idea, a pencil, a tick, the scales of accountability.

Bottom row: fewer than four criteria means a thank-you in the Acknowledgements. Red: a gift author is named without doing the work, a ghost author did the work but is not named.

Poll: is data collection alone enough for authorship? Expected: no.

Agree the author list at the protocol stage.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A declared interest is information. A hidden one is a scandal.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three panels: financial interests, non-financial interests, and the funding statement.

Non-financial interests are named in the ICMJE recommendations and disclosure form: personal relationships, guideline roles, unpaid roles in a society or advocacy group, academic rivalry.

Bottom left: having an interest is common, hiding it is the problem. Most journals use the ICMJE disclosure form.

Bottom right: Paper 2 states its funder had no role. Paper 1 states an internal grant.

Ask: a company paid your travel last year. Declare it? Expected: if in doubt, declare.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Plan data sharing at the protocol stage: the patient's consent form must allow it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Left: a staircase from closed (red) to open (green). Both papers sit on the second step, 'available on reasonable request'. The top step is an open repository with a DOI (digital object identifier, a permanent web link).

Right: four checks before you share. The patient's consent form and the ethics approval must allow it, the data are de-identified, the data dictionary and code come with them, and the paper has a data-sharing statement.

Ask: what must your consent form say today so you can share tomorrow?
:::

Always check your target journal.</div></div></div>
```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Use AI like a junior assistant: check everything, disclose it, keep patient data out.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two panels: allowed with care (green ticks) and never (red crosses). The footnote names the sources.

ICMJE Recommendations: AI tools cannot be authors. Authors disclose their use, in the cover letter and in the paper (Acknowledgements for writing help, Methods for data work), and remain responsible for the content. Reviewers must not upload a manuscript to a tool that cannot keep it confidential.

COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) position statement on authorship and AI tools: AI cannot take responsibility, so it cannot be an author. Authors disclose how the tool was used.

Publisher policies (Springer Nature, Elsevier, JAMA): no AI authors, disclosure of use, and limits on AI-generated images. Details differ, so check the target journal's current policy before submitting.

Ask: a colleague has a chatbot write the Discussion and submits it unread. Which rules does this break?

Participants' guide with the journal rules and links: AI\_Use\_Guidance.pdf (sent by email).
:::

## Integrity scenarios: green, amber or red?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 5 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Six short integrity scenarios from research practice (exercise sheet, Part A)
- Green: fine. Amber: fine only if fixed or disclosed. Red: misconduct
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Scenario 1

- Three day-3 fluid charts are lost. A resident enters the balances 'from memory'.
- Your colour?
:::

::::

**OUTPUT** Work alone (2 min) on scenarios 1, 3 and 4, then vote a colour in the poll. Scenarios 2, 5 and 6 at home
:::

::: {.notes}
Scenarios (20:25-20:30). Scenarios: s7\_exercises Part A.

2 minutes: everyone works alone on scenarios 1, 3 and 4. Then 3 minutes: one poll per scenario (green, amber, red), and call on one person from the largest and one from the smallest colour for a reason. Answers on the next slide.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}

- 'Remembered' values are invented data
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Scenario 3: red]{.neu-card-title}

- Gift authorship
- Seniority is not a contribution
:::

[Scenario 4: green and red]{.neu-card-title}

- Green: language polishing, checked and disclosed
- Red: patient spreadsheet in a public AI tool
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Red is misconduct. Scenarios 2, 5 and 6 are homework.
:::

::: {.notes}
All six answers: s7\_solutions Part A. Scenario 4 has two parts. The author stays responsible for the polished text. Identifiable patient data never go into a public AI tool.

Timing: within the 5 minutes of the scenarios.
:::

## Proposal builder 7: ethics, registration, feasibility, publication plan

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#055F56"}
PROPOSAL BUILDER · 15 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#055F56"}
- Proposal Part 4: ethics, registration, feasibility and publication plan (exercise sheet, Part B)
- The instructor first shows each block for the running example
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
Four blocks

- Patient's consent: needed? Who consents, who asks, when? (4 min)
- Registration and identifying file (3 min)
- Feasibility: biggest risk, one fix (3 min)
- Publication plan (5 min)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#055F56"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (1 to 2 min per block): write your own answer in Part B. Anything left: at home
:::

::: {.notes}
Proposal builder 7 (20:30-20:45). For each block: fill in Part B for the running example on screen, then 1 to 2 minutes for everyone to write their own answer alone, then call on two or three people. Answers: s7\_solutions Part B.

Watch for: 'consent will be obtained' with no who or when, chart reviews assumed exempt, recruitment taken from the sample size, CONSORT for a cohort.

Homework: Part 4 of their own proposal. Volunteers who want to present email the instructor by Wednesday 16 December.
:::

IMRaD first, then the STROBE map, Methods and Results, each with a worked example on Q1. The check practises both.

**KEY MESSAGE** Introduction narrows to your question. Discussion widens back to practice.
:::

::: {.notes}
The hourglass: wide at the top, narrow in the middle, wide at the bottom. Each section has its question on the right.

IMRaD: Introduction (why), Methods (what we did), Results (what we found), Discussion (what it means). The abstract and title summarise it.

The Introduction narrows to the question, the Discussion widens back to practice. Paper 1's Introduction is a three-paragraph funnel, and its Discussion opens by answering the question.

Today: Methods and Results. Next Saturday: Introduction, Discussion, abstract and title.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Start with your tables. Write the title last.
:::

::: {.notes}
Top row (grey outlines): the order readers read. Bottom row (coloured, numbered): the order writers write, with the reason under each step.

Writers start from the evidence: tables first, the title last.

For FLUID-ICU the tables already exist in your results pack, so your Results section starts from them.

Misconception: 'I must finish the Introduction before I can start'.
:::

## Methods: enough detail for someone to repeat it

::: {.neu-intro}
Methods say what you did. If a colleague could not redo the study from it, add detail.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Who and where]{.neu-card-title}

- Design, setting, dates
- Eligibility criteria
- Ethics approval and consent
- Registration number
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[What was done]{.neu-card-title}

- Intervention or exposure in full
- Variables defined
- Paper 1: staff training, daily pharmacist check
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Outcomes and size]{.neu-card-title}

- One primary outcome: how and when
- Sample size: assumptions and source
- Paper 2: no sample-size statement
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Statistical analysis]{.neu-card-title}

- A method for each comparison
- Estimate matches the test
- Missing data, multiple comparisons
- Software and version
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Give enough detail to repeat the study, and a method for every comparison.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four cards: who and where, what was done, outcomes and size, statistical analysis.

Good: Paper 1 describes its intervention well enough to replicate. To fix: Paper 2 gives no sample-size statement.

For FLUID-ICU, all the facts are in the results pack, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and the data dictionary.
:::

## STROBE for the FLUID-ICU paper: which item goes where

::: {.neu-intro}
STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology): the reporting checklist for cohorts.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Participants first, then each outcome as an effect size with its 95% CI.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four rules, each with an example from the papers.

1: participants first, as a flow. Paper 1 screened 1,201, randomised 50 and analysed 48 (2 withdrew consent).

2: effects with 95% CIs (red cross: 'p = 0.42, not significant'. Green tick: the difference with its CI, from Paper 1).

3: no interpretation. The Results report, the Discussion interprets. Paper 2 reports its results in the order of its aims.

4: one home per number. Text and tables must agree: Paper 1's text and Table 1 disagree on creatinine.

Before submitting, check every number against your results pack.
:::

::: {.notes}
One sentence per STROBE item, 13 to 17, all numbers from results pack Q1 (simulated). OR = odds ratio, HR = hazard ratio, CI = confidence interval.

Bottom bar: point out what is missing. No 'because', no 'significant', no reason why the OR shrank. That belongs in a Discussion.

This is the model for everyone's own Results in the workshop, whatever their question.

Poll: which item asks for crude and adjusted estimates? Expected: 16.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A reader should understand each table without reading the text.
:::

::: {.notes}
Left: Paper 1's Table 1, rebuilt. Right: what makes it stand alone (green ticks) and the errors in the papers (red cross).

A title that says what, in whom and when, n in every column header, units and summary in each row, footnotes for abbreviations. No p-values in a randomised trial's Table 1.

Errors in the papers: sodium printed in the wrong unit and a copy-pasted row (Paper 1), units written '\* 10\^3/L' (Paper 2).

Ask: what is wrong with a table titled 'Results'?
:::

## Worked example: FLUID-ICU Table 1 in one sentence

| Characteristic | Negative balance (n = 245) | Positive balance (n = 373) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Age, years, mean | 64.6 | 61.4 |
| SOFA score, median (IQR) | 6 (4 to 8) | 8 (6 to 10) |
| Vasopressor, n (%) | 61 (24.9%) | 205 (55.0%) |
| Mechanical ventilation, n (%) | 97 (39.6%) | 216 (57.9%) |
| Lactate, mmol/L, median (IQR) | 2.2 (1.4 to 3.0) | 2.9 (1.9 to 4.0) |
| Heart failure, n (%) | 54 (22.0%) | 43 (11.5%) |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Simulated data (results pack Q1, Table 1). Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. Interquartile range (IQR). Sentence: 'Patients with a positive balance were sicker at baseline.'
:::

::: {.notes}
The table shows six rows of Table 1 for Q1. From it, one Results sentence (STROBE 14): 'Patients with a positive balance were sicker at baseline (median SOFA 8 vs 6, vasopressors 55.0% vs 24.9%) and less often had heart failure (11.5% vs 22.0%).'

The sentence describes, it does not test: no p-values.
:::

Left: the FLUID-ICU Kaplan-Meier figure from Session 6 (Q1, simulated data), drawn the way a paper should show it. Right: what makes it stand alone (green ticks) and an error from Paper 1 (red cross).

The legend under the plot says what is shown, in whom, and what the shaded bands mean. Axes are labelled with units, the groups are named on the plot, and the numbers at risk sit under the curve.

Paper 1 cites the wrong figure numbers in its text: check every call-out before submitting.

Ask: if this figure were copied into a slide without the text, what would a reader still understand?

## Check: Methods, Results or Discussion?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'We used logistic regression adjusted for SOFA score and age.'
- 'Of 620 patients enrolled, 618 had a day-3 fluid balance.'
- 'This may be because sicker patients received more fluid.'
- 'Lactate was missing in 15.0% of patients and was imputed.'
- '28-day mortality was higher with a positive balance (adjusted OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.59).'
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Methods
- Results
- Discussion
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One poll vote per sentence
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (21:32-21:35). One poll per sentence. Show the results, then the answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: Methods, Results or Discussion?

| Sentence | Section | Why |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Logistic regression adjusted for SOFA and age | Methods | It says how we analysed |
| 618 of 620 had a day-3 balance | Results | It reports the participants |
| 'This may be because...' | Discussion | It explains a finding |
| Lactate missing in 15.0%, imputed | Methods and Results | How it was handled is Methods. How many were missing is Results |
| Adjusted OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.59 | Results | An estimate with its CI |

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Methods say what we did. Results say what we found. The Discussion explains it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The table gives the section and the reason for each sentence.

Sentence 4 is the trick: how missing data were handled is Methods, how many were missing is Results.

Sentence 3 is the classic error: interpretation in the Results.

Timing: within the 3 minutes of the check.
:::

INDIVIDUAL TASK · 25 min

:::: {.columns}

- STROBE 15 and 16: deaths or events per group, then crude and adjusted estimates with 95% CIs
- Model: the Q1 worked examples from 7.3. Every number from your own pack
:::

The five questions

- Q1 Fluid balance and 28-day death
- Q2 Fluid balance and AKI (acute kidney injury)
- Q3 Fluid balance and ventilator-free days
- Q4 Lactate, death and missing data
- Q5 Fluid balance and ICU stay (survivors)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#0B376C"}
**OUTPUT** Work alone (25 min). Ask questions in the chat at any time
:::

::: {.notes}
Workshop part 1 (21:35-22:00). Keep a visible timer. Everyone writes the Results of their own question, alone.

Answer questions in the chat. At about 21:50, ask one volunteer per question (Q1 to Q5) to paste one sentence in the chat, and comment on each in one line.

Per question: Q1: write in your own words, do not copy the worked example. Q2: report the number with AKI per group. Q3: ventilator-free days count death as zero. Q4: report both complete-case and imputed estimates. Q5: survivors only, medians and IQR (interquartile range).

Prompts: 'Is there a number without its CI?' 'Is there an adjective that should be a number?' 'Any interpretation?'
:::

At about 22:15, ask everyone to run the four checks on the right and post one problem they found.

At home everyone finishes the Results, Table 1 and one main table or figure, all from their own pack.

Other sections may be added, but only the Results must be submitted.

## Key words of Session 7

| Term | In plain words |
|:---|:---|
| Deferred consent | Enrol first in an emergency, ask for consent as soon as possible (committee-approved) |
| Pseudonymised data | Names replaced by a code. An identifying file can still link back to the patient |
| Fabrication, falsification, plagiarism (FFP) | The three forms of research misconduct |
| International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) criteria | The four conditions every author must meet |
| Conflict of interest | Anything that could be seen to influence your judgement. Declare it |
| Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) | Reporting checklist for observational studies: Methods items 4 to 12, Results 13 to 17 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Full glossary (English-Vietnamese): Glossary\_EN\_VN.pdf, emailed with the Session 1 files a week before the course
:::

::: {.notes}
Key words (22:20-22:22). The table gives each term in full, with its abbreviation, and a plain-words meaning. Read each term, call on someone to explain it, then read the right-hand column.

The full glossary (Course/References/Glossary\_EN\_VN.pdf) was emailed a week before Session 1. Resend it on request.
:::

## Check: register or not?

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 2 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- A randomised trial of restrictive vs usual fluids in septic shock
- A systematic review of fluid strategies in sepsis
- A retrospective cohort from ICU charts (like FLUID-ICU)
- A clinical audit of fluid-balance charting against the unit standard
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
Choose

- Must register
- Should register
- Recommended
- Not needed
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One poll vote per scenario
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra check. One poll per scenario. Show the results, then the answers on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: register or not?

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Trial: must]{.neu-card-title}

- In a trial registry
- before patient 1
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Review: should]{.neu-card-title}

- On PROSPERO
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Cohort: recommended]{.neu-card-title}

- Not required
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Audit: not needed]{.neu-card-title}

- Local approval
- not a research registry
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Register a trial before the first patient. An audit needs local approval only.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four cards, one answer each.

Scenario 4: an audit goes through the quality office, not a registry. To publish it as research, ask the ethics committee first.

Timing: within the 2 minutes of the check.

## CRediT: say who did what

::: {.neu-intro}
CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy): 14 standard roles that journals now ask for.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Some of the 14 roles]{.neu-card-title}

- Conceptualization
- Methodology
- Investigation
- Formal analysis
- Writing (original draft)
- Writing (review and editing)
- Supervision
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Paper 1 did it]{.neu-card-title}

- NB: Writing (original draft)
- CS: Methodology, Formal analysis
- SDB: Conceptualization, Supervision, Funding acquisition
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Your proposal]{.neu-card-title}

- Agree the author list now
- Write each person's roles
- Revisit before submission
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Transparent roles prevent gift and ghost authorship.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Three cards: the roles, Paper 1's statement, and what to do in your proposal.

CRediT names who did what (14 roles). It does not replace the ICMJE criteria.

Ask each participant to write who would do what in their own proposal.
:::
